title: Response temporal consistency lab
content:
Scratchpad: temporal consistency experiments for instruction-following responses

Context / why this: we see customers report that the same instruction phrased identically yields different structural outputs across repeated calls (esp. with streaming tokens + small temperature). Hypothesis: implicit state (system+previous session) + decoding nondeterminism + prefix caching interplay create surface-level drift. Want a small prompt-library and few-shot bank to detect and reduce drift in production (hosted API + dedicated).

Goals:
- Define compact few-shot patterns that anchor response shape (not content).
- Create lightweight checks that catch structural drift (e.g., JSON schema order, bullet count).
- Experiment with prefix locking / deterministic seeds + cache warming to measure effect.

Key questions (notes to self):
- Does adding an explicit "response schema" example reduce helpfulness? tradeoffs?
- How much does streaming affect final punctuation / trailing list items?
- Can we make a 3-shot scaffold that generalizes across topics?

Quick experiments (one-off runs):
1) Minimal anchor (control): system: "You are a concise assistant." prompt: single instruction "List 4 pros and cons of X." (temp 0.0)
Observed: sometimes returns 3 bullets, sometimes 5. Failure: length variation.

2) Shape-anchored few-shot: preface with 2 examples (topic A, topic B) showing exactly 4 bullets and explicit closing line "END-OF-LIST". Prompt: topic C.
Observed: higher compliance (4 bullets) but occasional newline + extra commentary after END-OF-LIST.

3) Schema-first: preface: JSON schema + one example mapping. Prompt: "Return JSON that matches schema".
Observed: structurally consistent but content collapsed into single line for long fields (loss of readability). Some models truncated keys when token-limited.

Few-shot bank (candidate sets) - format: 
- Set A (concise bullets)
  Example 1: 
  Q: "List 4 benefits of server-side caching."
  A: "- Faster response
- Lower DB load
- Better scalability
- Reduced cost
END-OF-LIST"

  Example 2: similar for different topic.

- Set B (JSON schema anchor)
  Example: 
  Q: "Summarize research notes."
  A: "{\n  \"title\": \"Notes\",\n  \"summary\": \"one-paragraph summary...\"\n}\nEND-OF-JSON"

Failure cases observed (catalog):
- Trailing commentary after anchor token (END-OF-LIST/END-OF-JSON) when prompt includes ambiguous politeness markers.
- Partial list (3/4) when input includes long context + token limit triggered.
- Order variance in keys when asking for unordered sets; deterministic ordering sometimes desirable.
- Very small temperature (0.0) reduces variety but does not fully eliminate list-length drift.

Debug traces to capture per-run for repro: model name, exact input bytes, seed (if supported), tokenization length, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache hit rate, timed latency per chunk. Save these with HAR-like minimal record.

Experiment ideas (next runs):
- 'prefix-lock' variant: send anchor few-shot on first request, then only content in subsequent warm calls to test cache effect. Compare to always-sending anchor.
- deterministic decode w/ forced eos token derived from anchor (see PR #12 linked).
- fallback policy test: when output fails schema check, auto-retry with stricter anchor and lower temp. Measure 99th percentile added latency.

Mini-protocol for building prompt-library entries (for productizing):
1) "intent" (one-line): e.g., "Enumerate pros/cons with fixed length"
2) anchor style: bullets | numbered | JSON-schema | labeled sections
3) canonical few-shot examples: 2-3 per anchor style
4) failure modes: short description + steps to reproduce
5) mitigations: retry policy, schema-check, cache-warm
6) metric to track: structural-error-rate, median latency, cost delta

Notes / rough heuristics: 
- Prefer explicit terminators: explicit tokens (END-OF-LIST) > punctuation alone.
- JSON anchors help but increase token overhead; balance with model token limits.
- Avoid anthropomorphic phrasing in anchor examples (e.g., "I think") — it introduces extra commentary.

To-do (short):
- [ ] run 500-sample A/B on hosted-api (gpt-like-16k equivalent) comparing Set A vs Set B across 10 topics (Evan owning experiment harness).
- [ ] add schema-check function to console (product-ops ticket) to auto-detect structural regression. Link once created.
- [ ] draft short internal README for solutions-eng with safe fallbacks.

References / links (quick):
- Slack thread: #ml-evals thread "response-drift-examples" (recent pinned images)
- Linear: RED-341 (linked)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/repro-evals/pull/12 (temp decode experiments)

Random scratch lines: 
- "If model pads with filler bullets, try explicit negative example showing what not to do."
- "Test with both streaming and non-streaming; streaming may show partial structure early that affects clean-up."

End of scratchpad. Will iterate; keep this file as living notes.
